meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Death is nothing at all. I have only slipped away into the next room'?
meta.ogDescription: Canon Henry Scott Holland, 1910. The funeral reading is half of a sermon that also calls death 'the King of Terrors'.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1847–1918 · Canon of St Paul’s Cathedral, later Regius Professor of Divinity at Oxford
answer.sourceLine: Holland preached this in St Paul’s Cathedral on Sunday 15 May 1910, after the death of King Edward VII, in a sermon called The King of Terrors. Two things the funeral-card version hides: the original reads ‘Death is nothing at all. It does not count. I have only slipped away…’, and Holland is not speaking in his own voice — he is imagining what the dead person’s face says to the mourner, as one of two opposed views of death he goes on to refuse to choose between.

source.heading: A sermon with two halves

docMeta.dd: ‘The King of Terrors’, in Facts of the Faith
Longmans, Green & Co., London, 1919 — sermon begins p. 124, passage on p. 126
St Paul’s Cathedral, London, Sunday 15 May 1910 (Whitsunday), after the death of King Edward VII
Verified — but routinely quoted without its context

source.excerpt: But, then, there is another aspect altogether which death can wear for us. It is that which first comes to us, perhaps, as we look down upon the quiet face, so cold and white, of one who has been very near and dear to us. There it lies in possession of its own secret. It knows it all. So we seem to feel. And what the face says in its sweet silence to us as a last message from the one whom we loved is: "Death is nothing at all. It does not count. I have only slipped away into the next room. Nothing has happened. Everything remains exactly as it was."
trail: The sermon is printed in Holland’s Facts of the Faith (1919), scanned in full at the Internet Archive ↗ — a posthumous collection ‘of sermons not hitherto published in book form’, edited by Christopher Cheshire. The passage sits on p. 126, inside the sermon the contents page lists as ‘The King of Terrors’.

Wikisource’s edition of the sermon ↗ dates and places it: ‘A sermon preached in St Paul’s Cathedral, London, Sunday 15th May 1910… following the death of King Edward VII, whose coffin lay in state in Westminster Hall from 17 to 19 May.’ The sermon’s own text agrees — Holland says ‘to-day the white light of Pentecost pours itself around us’, and speaks of the coffin ‘as it lies in Westminster Hall’.

That the passage misrepresents the sermon is not our inference. Wikipedia’s article on Holland ↗ records that ‘the frequent use of this passage has provoked some criticism that it fails to accurately reflect either Holland’s theology as a whole, or the focus of the sermon in particular’, citing John Heidt’s ‘The King of Terrors: The Theology of Henry Scott Holland’ in Contemporary Review (March 2000).
source.excerptNote: The quotation marks are Holland’s own. The famous passage is what he imagines the dead face saying — a voice he introduces, not a creed he announces. The funeral reading begins at ‘Death is nothing at all’ and silently drops the sentence that follows it.

author.name: Henry Scott Holland
author.heading: About Henry Scott Holland
author.metaLine: 1847–1918 · English priest, Christian socialist & Regius Professor of Divinity
author.bio: Henry Scott Holland (1847–1918) was born near Ledbury in Herefordshire, educated at Eton and Balliol, and elected a fellow of Christ Church, Oxford. In 1884 he left Oxford to become a canon of St Paul’s Cathedral, where he preached this sermon; he declined the bishopric of Norwich in 1893 and returned to Oxford as Regius Professor of Divinity. He founded the Christian Social Union, and was slow to publish — nine volumes of his sermons appeared in his lifetime, and this one only posthumously.

misattribution.heading: Not a misattribution — a missing half
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is credited with these words; Holland really wrote them. What goes wrong is the framing, and it goes wrong in four repeatable ways.

items.why: The sermon reads ‘Death is nothing at all. It does not count. I have only slipped away into the next room.’ The funeral reading drops the middle sentence, which is why the clipped form is the one people search for.

items.who: Henry Scott Holland, speaking for himself
items.why: He is not. Holland writes that this is ‘what the face says in its sweet silence to us as a last message from the one whom we loved’ — the words are given to the dead, in quotation marks, as a mourner’s imagining.

It is a sermon about a contradiction. Holland opens ‘I suppose all of us hover between two ways of regarding death, which appear to be in hopeless contradiction with each other’, spends the first half on death as ‘the supreme and irrevocable disaster’, and concludes: ‘Our task is to deny neither judgment, but to combine both. The contrasted experiences are equally real, equally valid.’

That is the opening line, not the sermon’s name. Facts of the Faith lists it as ‘The King of Terrors’; it is also widely cited as ‘Death the King of Terrors’. Either way the title names the terror, not the comfort.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Holland’s, from p. 126 of Facts of the Faith ↗ — but they are one side of an argument he deliberately left unresolved, spoken in a voice that is not his own.

context.heading: Preached beside a king’s coffin
lead: Whitsunday 1910 fell between the death of Edward VII and his lying-in-state, and Holland preached into that gap. ‘To-day the white light of Pentecost pours itself around us,’ he told the congregation, ‘yet the white light breaks itself against the blackness of a closed coffin… and its very pomp of state makes its silence more sinister yet.’ The consoling passage was never meant to stand alone; it was the second of two moods he set against each other in front of a nation in mourning.
context.detailsSummary: How he tried to hold both at once
detailsBody: Holland does not withdraw the comfort. He calls the mood that produces it a ‘true experience’ that ‘gave us authentic intelligence’, and says it is ‘our reasonable act of faith to stand by our highest experience… even when its light has faded out of our lives’. But he is equally blunt that it will fade: ‘Alas! it will pass from us… Once again the old terror will come down upon us.’ His answer is not to pick a side but to reconcile them through the idea of growth — that we are ‘in a condition of process’ of which life on earth is only the preliminary stage. Read whole, it is a far stranger and more demanding sermon than the card it became.
context.pull: Our task is to deny neither judgment, but to combine both.

sourcesVerified.claim: Facts of the Faith (Longmans, Green & Co., 1919) contains the sermon 'The King of Terrors' from p. 124; on p. 126 it reads 'And what the face says in its sweet silence to us as a last message from the one whom we loved is: "Death is nothing at all. It does not count. I have only slipped away into the next room..."'. The sermon opens 'I suppose all of us hover between two ways of regarding death' and concludes 'Our task is to deny neither judgment, but to combine both.' Its text is 1 John 3:2-3, and a footnote identifies the royal coffin as King Edward VII's.

Wikisource's edition headnote: 'A sermon preached in St Paul's Cathedral, London, Sunday 15th May 1910. The sermon was preached following the death of King Edward VII, whose coffin lay in state in Westminster Hall from 17 to 19 May.'

Holland lived 27 January 1847 - 17 March 1918, became a canon of St Paul's Cathedral in 1884, declined the see of Norwich in 1893, and was Regius Professor of Divinity at Oxford; the article also states that frequent use of this passage 'has provoked some criticism that it fails to accurately reflect either Holland's theology as a whole, or the focus of the sermon in particular'.

1 John 3:2 (KJV) reads 'Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.' - matching the sermon's printed text.
